claim: Treatment of chow-fed mice with leptin suppressed feeding behavior and caused decreased body mass.
source: Indeed, treatment of chow-fed mice with leptin suppressed feeding behavior and caused decreased body mass (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating body mass changes after leptin treatment in chow-fed mice.

claim: HFD-fed mice failed to respond to leptin.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed mice failed to respond to leptin (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating lack of body mass change after leptin treatment in HFD-fed mice.

claim: Feeding a HFD caused JNK3 phosphorylation and activation in the hypothalamus.
source: This analysis demonstrated that feeding a HFD caused JNK3 phosphorylation and activation in the hypothalamus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating phospho-JNK3 levels in hypothalamus of HFD-fed mice.

claim: Mapk10-/- mice gained similar body mass to WT mice when fed a chow diet.
source: We found that Mapk10-/- mice gained similar body mass when fed a CD, but these mice gained significantly greater mass when fed a HFD compared with WT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by body mass measurements shown in Figure 1C comparing WT and Mapk10-/- mice on chow diet.

claim: Mapk10-/- mice gained significantly greater mass when fed a HFD compared with WT mice.
source: We found that Mapk10-/- mice gained similar body mass when fed a CD, but these mice gained significantly greater mass when fed a HFD compared with WT mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by body mass measurements shown in Figure 1C comparing WT and Mapk10-/- mice on HFD.

claim: The greater HFD-induced body mass in Mapk10-/- mice was caused by increased fat and lean mass.
source: 1H-MRS analysis demonstrated that the greater HFD-induced body mass was caused by increased fat and lean mass (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by 1H-MRS analysis data shown in Figure 1D measuring fat and lean mass in HFD-fed mice.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased liver, skeletal muscle, heart, and adipose tissue mass compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Indeed, HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased liver, skeletal muscle, heart, and adipose tissue mass compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by organ mass measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Microscopic examination of tissue sections demonstrated increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes and increased hepatic steatosis in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1E of adipose tissue sections.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased hepatic steatosis compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Microscopic examination of tissue sections demonstrated increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes and increased hepatic steatosis in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 1E of liver sections.

claim: Mapk10 gene ablation selectively increased consumption of a HFD, but not a CD.
source: These studies demonstrated that Mapk10 gene ablation selectively increased consumption of a HFD, but not a CD (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage analysis data shown in Figure 1F measuring food consumption.

claim: The HFD-selective hyperphagia was observed within 2 days of consuming the HFD.
source: Time course analysis demonstrated that the HFD-selective hyperphagia was observed within 2 days of consuming the HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and was detected prior to the development of obesity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by time course data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A measuring food consumption over days.

claim: The HFD-selective hyperphagia was detected prior to the development of obesity.
source: Time course analysis demonstrated that the HFD-selective hyperphagia was observed within 2 days of consuming the HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and was detected prior to the development of obesity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by body composition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B measured at 3 days of HFD feeding.

claim: No significant changes in VO2, VCO2, or energy expenditure were detected in the HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.
source: No significant changes in VO2, VCO2, or energy expenditure were detected in the HFD-fed mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hyperphagia contributes to the increased obesity of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: These data suggest that hyperphagia contributes to the increased obesity of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased food consumption and increased obesity in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.

claim: WT and Mapk10-/- mice gained similar body mass when fed the same amount of food.
source: We found that WT and Mapk10-/- mice gained similar body mass when fed the same amount of food (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by pair-feeding experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hyperphagia accounts for the increased HFD-induced obesity of Mapk10-/- mice compared with WT mice.
source: These data demonstrate that hyperphagia accounts for the increased HFD-induced obesity of Mapk10-/- mice compared with WT mice.
evidence: Inferred from pair-feeding experiment showing equal body mass gain when food intake is matched.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased hyperinsulinemia compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Consequences of the increased HFD feeding behavior of Mapk10-/- mice include increased hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia (Figure 1G), increased blood lipid concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), decreased glucose tolerance (Figure 1H), and increased insulin resistance (Figure 1I) when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
evidence: Supported by blood insulin measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased hyperleptinemia compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Consequences of the increased HFD feeding behavior of Mapk10-/- mice include increased hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia (Figure 1G), increased blood lipid concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), decreased glucose tolerance (Figure 1H), and increased insulin resistance (Figure 1I) when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
evidence: Supported by blood leptin measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased blood lipid concentrations compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Consequences of the increased HFD feeding behavior of Mapk10-/- mice include increased hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia (Figure 1G), increased blood lipid concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), decreased glucose tolerance (Figure 1H), and increased insulin resistance (Figure 1I) when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
evidence: Supported by blood lipid measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited decreased glucose tolerance compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Consequences of the increased HFD feeding behavior of Mapk10-/- mice include increased hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia (Figure 1G), increased blood lipid concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), decreased glucose tolerance (Figure 1H), and increased insulin resistance (Figure 1I) when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased insulin resistance compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: Consequences of the increased HFD feeding behavior of Mapk10-/- mice include increased hyperinsulinemia and hyperleptinemia (Figure 1G), increased blood lipid concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), decreased glucose tolerance (Figure 1H), and increased insulin resistance (Figure 1I) when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
evidence: Supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: No significant differences between CD-fed WT and Mapk10-/- mice were detected in hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp studies.
source: No significant differences between CD-fed WT and Mapk10-/- mice were detected (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2A-F for CD-fed mice.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose infusion rate compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose infusion rate (a measure of whole body insulin sensitivity), reduced glucose turnover, reduced whole body glycolysis, increased hepatic glucose production, and decreased hepatic insulin action compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose turnover compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose infusion rate (a measure of whole body insulin sensitivity), reduced glucose turnover, reduced whole body glycolysis, increased hepatic glucose production, and decreased hepatic insulin action compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced whole body glycolysis compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose infusion rate (a measure of whole body insulin sensitivity), reduced glucose turnover, reduced whole body glycolysis, increased hepatic glucose production, and decreased hepatic insulin action compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly increased hepatic glucose production compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose infusion rate (a measure of whole body insulin sensitivity), reduced glucose turnover, reduced whole body glycolysis, increased hepatic glucose production, and decreased hepatic insulin action compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly decreased hepatic insulin action compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice showed significantly reduced glucose infusion rate (a measure of whole body insulin sensitivity), reduced glucose turnover, reduced whole body glycolysis, increased hepatic glucose production, and decreased hepatic insulin action compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mapk10-/- mice exhibit a profound defect in glycemic regulation compared with WT mice when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
source: These data demonstrate that Mapk10-/- mice exhibit a profound defect in glycemic regulation compared with WT mice when fed a HFD, but not a CD.
evidence: Inferred from multiple measurements of glucose metabolism showing defects only in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.

claim: The increased adipose tissue mass of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice was associated with increased adipose tissue infiltration by F4/80+ macrophages.
source: The increased adipose tissue mass of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed control mice was associated with increased adipose tissue infiltration by F4/80+ macrophages (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited markedly increased expression of macrophage marker genes (Emr1 (F4/80) & Cd68) compared with HFD-fed control mice.
source: Indeed, gene expression analysis identified markedly increased expression of macrophage marker genes (Emr1 (F4/80) & Cd68), increased expression of genes associated with M1-like macrophage polarization (Ccl2, Il1b, Il6 & Tnf), and decreased expression of genes associated with M2-like macrophage polarization (Arg1, Mgl2, Mrc1 & Mrc2) in the adipose tissue of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed control mice (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased expression of genes associated with M1-like macrophage polarization (Ccl2, Il1b, Il6 & Tnf) compared with HFD-fed control mice.
source: Indeed, gene expression analysis identified markedly increased expression of macrophage marker genes (Emr1 (F4/80) & Cd68), increased expression of genes associated with M1-like macrophage polarization (Ccl2, Il1b, Il6 & Tnf), and decreased expression of genes associated with M2-like macrophage polarization (Arg1, Mgl2, Mrc1 & Mrc2) in the adipose tissue of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed control mice (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited decreased expression of genes associated with M2-like macrophage polarization (Arg1, Mgl2, Mrc1 & Mrc2) compared with HFD-fed control mice.
source: Indeed, gene expression analysis identified markedly increased expression of macrophage marker genes (Emr1 (F4/80) & Cd68), increased expression of genes associated with M1-like macrophage polarization (Ccl2, Il1b, Il6 & Tnf), and decreased expression of genes associated with M2-like macrophage polarization (Arg1, Mgl2, Mrc1 & Mrc2) in the adipose tissue of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed control mice (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: JNK3 deficiency promotes increased adipose tissue inflammation in HFD-fed mice.
source: These data indicate that JNK3 deficiency promotes increased adipose tissue inflammation in HFD-fed mice.
evidence: Inferred from increased macrophage infiltration and pro-inflammatory gene expression in adipose tissue of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.

claim: The increase in inflammation contributes to the glucose intolerant and insulin resistant phenotype of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: It is likely that this increase in inflammation contributes to the glucose intolerant and insulin resistant phenotype of HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Brestoff and Artis, 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the association between inflammation and metabolic dysfunction, supported by citation to Brestoff and Artis, 2015.

claim: Low concentrations of leptin were detected in the blood when WT and Mapk10-/- mice were fed a CD.
source: Low concentrations of leptin were detected in the blood when WT and Mapk10-/- mice were fed a CD (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by blood leptin measurements shown in Figure 1G for CD-fed mice.

claim: The blood leptin concentration was increased when mice were fed a HFD and was significantly greater in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: The blood leptin concentration was increased when these mice were fed a HFD and was significantly greater in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by blood leptin measurements shown in Figure 1G for HFD-fed mice.

claim: Changes in the amount of leptin circulating in the blood correlate with differences in obesity.
source: These changes in the amount of leptin circulating in the blood correlate, as expected, with differences in obesity (Friedman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Friedman, 2014 establishing the relationship between leptin and obesity.

claim: Leptin signaling may be suppressed in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.
source: This analysis suggested that leptin signaling may be suppressed in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of hyperleptinemia and hyperphagia in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice, which is inconsistent with normal leptin function.

claim: Intracerebroventricular administration of leptin decreased the body mass of WT mice, but not Mapk10-/- mice.
source: We found that intracerebroventricular administration of leptin decreased the body mass of WT mice, but not Mapk10-/- mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by body mass measurements after leptin treatment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Leptin decreased Agrp and Npy expression in WT mice, but not Mapk10-/- mice.
source: Measurement of hypothalamic gene expression demonstrated that leptin decreased Agrp and Npy expression in WT mice, but not Mapk10-/- mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Leptin caused increased Pomc and Socs3 gene expression in both WT and Mapk10-/- mice.
source: In contrast, leptin caused increased Pomc and Socs3 gene expression in both WT and Mapk10-/- mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mapk10-/- mice exhibit a selective deficiency in leptin regulation of Agrp and Npy expression.
source: These data indicate that Mapk10-/- mice exhibit a selective deficiency in leptin regulation of Agrp and Npy expression.
evidence: Inferred from the differential response to leptin treatment between WT and Mapk10-/- mice for Agrp/Npy versus Pomc/Socs3.

claim: HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice exhibited increased Agrp and Npy expression compared with HFD-fed WT mice.
source: This analysis demonstrated increased Agrp and Npy expression in HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice compared with HFD-fed WT mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No significant difference in Pomc and Socs3 gene expression between HFD-fed WT and Mapk10-/- mice was detected.
source: In contrast, no significant difference in Pomc and Socs3 gene expression between HFD-fed WT and Mapk10-/- mice was detected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: JNK3 deficiency caused a selective defect in leptin signaling.
source: These observations indicate that JNK3 deficiency caused a selective defect in leptin signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effects on Agrp/Npy but not Pomc/Socs3 expression in response to leptin.

claim: The difference in body mass between HFD-fed LepRΔJ3 and LepRWT mice was caused by increased fat mass.
source: 1H-MRS analysis showed that the difference in body mass was caused by increased fat mass (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by 1H-MRS analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mapk10 gene ablation in LEPRb+ neurons caused no change in CD food consumption, but caused increased HFD food consumption.
source: Metabolic cage analysis demonstrated that Mapk10 gene ablation in LEPRb+ neurons caused no change in CD food consumption, but caused increased HFD food consumption (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by food consumption measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increase in HFD consumption in LepRΔJ3 mice was not associated with changes in VO2, VCO2, or energy expenditure.
source: This increase in HFD consumption was not associated with changes in VO2, VCO2, or energy expenditure (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: JNK3 in LEPRb+ neurons of HFD-fed mice regulates feeding behavior, but not other aspects of energy balance.
source: JNK3 in LEPRb+ neurons of HFD-fed mice therefore regulates feeding behavior, but not other aspects of energy balance.
evidence: Inferred from the selective effect on food consumption without changes in energy expenditure in LepRΔJ3 mice.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in LepRb+ neurons caused increased HFD-induced hepatic steatosis.
source: Moreover, JNK3 deficiency in LepRb+ neurons caused increased HFD-induced hepatic steatosis (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in feeding behavior compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice.
source: We found that JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in feeding behavior, glucose intolerance, blood glucose concentration, hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and hepatic steatosis compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice (Figure 5A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by food consumption data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in glucose intolerance compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice.
source: We found that JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in feeding behavior, glucose intolerance, blood glucose concentration, hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and hepatic steatosis compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice (Figure 5A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in blood glucose concentration compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice.
source: We found that JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in feeding behavior, glucose intolerance, blood glucose concentration, hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and hepatic steatosis compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice (Figure 5A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice.
source: We found that JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in feeding behavior, glucose intolerance, blood glucose concentration, hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and hepatic steatosis compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice (Figure 5A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in hepatic steatosis compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice.
source: We found that JNK3 deficiency in POMC neurons of HFD-fed mice caused no significant changes in feeding behavior, glucose intolerance, blood glucose concentration, hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and hepatic steatosis compared with control Pomc-cre (PomcWT) mice (Figure 5A,C,E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased feeding compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice.
source: In contrast, JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased feeding, increased glucose intolerance, increased blood glucose concentration, increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and increased hepatic steatosis compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice (Figure 5B,D,F).
evidence: Supported by food consumption data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased glucose intolerance compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice.
source: In contrast, JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased feeding, increased glucose intolerance, increased blood glucose concentration, increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and increased hepatic steatosis compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice (Figure 5B,D,F).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased blood glucose concentration compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice.
source: In contrast, JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased feeding, increased glucose intolerance, increased blood glucose concentration, increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and increased hepatic steatosis compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice (Figure 5B,D,F).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice.
source: In contrast, JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased feeding, increased glucose intolerance, increased blood glucose concentration, increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and increased hepatic steatosis compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice (Figure 5B,D,F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased hepatic steatosis compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice.
source: In contrast, JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons in HFD-fed mice caused increased feeding, increased glucose intolerance, increased blood glucose concentration, increased hypertrophy of white and brown adipocytes, and increased hepatic steatosis compared with control Agrp-cre (AgrpWT) mice (Figure 5B,D,F).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The VO2, VCO2, and energy expenditure of HFD-fed AgrpΔJ3 mice and PomcΔJ3 mice were similar to control mice.
source: Metabolic cage analysis demonstrated that the VO2, VCO2, and energy expenditure of HFD-fed Agrp∆J3 mice and Pomc∆J3 mice were similar to control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolic cage measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: JNK3 in AgRP neurons, but not POMC neurons, acts to suppress HFD consumption.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that JNK3 in AgRP neurons, but not POMC neurons, acts to suppress HFD consumption.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phenotypes of AgrpΔJ3 and PomcΔJ3 mice on HFD.

claim: JNK3 deficiency caused no change in mIPSC frequency or amplitude in CD-fed and HFD-fed mice.
source: This analysis demonstrated that JNK3 deficiency caused no change in mIPSC frequency or amplitude in CD-fed and HFD-fed mice (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: JNK3 deficiency caused no change in mEPSC frequency or amplitude in CD-fed mice.
source: Similarly, JNK3 deficiency caused no change in mEPSC frequency or amplitude in CD-fed mice (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E-H for CD-fed mice.

claim: HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice demonstrated increased mEPSC amplitudes in the absence of changes in mEPSC frequency.
source: In contrast, HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice demonstrated increased mEPSC amplitudes in the absence of changes in mEPSC frequency (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6E-H for HFD-fed mice.

claim: The mEPSC currents in AgRP neurons were mediated by AMPA receptors.
source: Studies using the selective antagonist DNQX demonstrated that these mEPSC currents were mediated by AMPA receptors in AgRP neurons (Figure 6-figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data using DNQX shown in Figure 6-figure supplement 1.

claim: JNK3 deficiency leads to altered excitatory transmission onto AgRP neurons compared to WT mice when fed a HFD.
source: Together, these data indicate that JNK3 deficiency leads to altered excitatory transmission onto AgRP neurons compared to WT mice when fed a HFD.
evidence: Inferred from the increased mEPSC amplitude in HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice.

claim: The altered excitatory transmission in JNK3-deficient AgRP neurons is consistent with the increased expression of AgRP and NPY and the increased food consumption observed in HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice.
source: This finding is consistent with the increased expression of AgRP and NPY (Figure 3C) and the increased food consumption (Figure 1F) observed in HFD-fed JNK3-deficient compared to HFD-fed WT mice.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between electrophysiological changes and behavioral/molecular phenotypes.

claim: The arcuate nucleus (ARC) in the hypothalamus plays a key role in the regulation of energy balance.
source: It is established that the arcuate nucleus (ARC) in the hypothalamus plays a key role in the regulation of energy balance (Cone, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cone, 2005 establishing this role of the ARC.

claim: AgRP neurons in the ARC mediate orexigenic signals, including neuropeptide Y (NPY), agouti-related peptide (AgRP), and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA).
source: AgRP neurons in the ARC mediate orexigenic signals, including neuropeptide Y (NPY), agouti-related peptide (AgRP), and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) that project to POMC neurons in the ARC and to secondary response neurons in many brain regions, including the lateral hypothalamus (LH) and the paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about AgRP neuron function.

claim: POMC neurons mediate anorexigenic signals, including cocaine and amphetamine regulated transcript (CART) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-derived α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH).
source: In contrast, POMC neurons mediate anorexigenic signals, including cocaine and amphetamine regulated transcript (CART) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-derived α-melanocyte stimulating hormone (α-MSH).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about POMC neuron function.

claim: α-MSH acts as an agonist of the melanocortin receptors MC3R and MC4R on secondary response neurons to inhibit feeding and increase energy expenditure.
source: POMC neurons project to many brain areas, including the PVN and LH in the hypothalamus where α-MSH acts as an agonist of the melanocortin receptors MC3R and MC4R on secondary response neurons to inhibit feeding and increase energy expenditure.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about α-MSH function.

claim: The action of α-MSH is antagonized by AgRP.
source: Importantly, this action of α-MSH is antagonized by AgRP.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about AgRP function.

claim: POMC neurons receive inhibitory GABAergic input from AgRP neurons.
source: Moreover, POMC neurons receive inhibitory GABAergic input from AgRP neurons.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about AgRP-POMC neuron interactions.

claim: AgRP and POMC neurons act together to balance food consumption, energy expenditure and nutrient homeostasis.
source: Consequently, AgRP and POMC neurons act together to balance food consumption, energy expenditure and nutrient homeostasis (Cone, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cone, 2005 and draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Leptin activates POMC neurons.
source: Thus, leptin activates POMC neurons (Cowley et al., 2001) and inhibits AgRP neurons (Takahashi and Cone, 2005) leading to reduced food consumption and increased energy expenditure.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cowley et al., 2001.

claim: Leptin inhibits AgRP neurons.
source: Thus, leptin activates POMC neurons (Cowley et al., 2001) and inhibits AgRP neurons (Takahashi and Cone, 2005) leading to reduced food consumption and increased energy expenditure.
evidence: Supported by citation to Takahashi and Cone, 2005.

claim: Leptin action leads to reduced food consumption and increased energy expenditure.
source: Thus, leptin activates POMC neurons (Cowley et al., 2001) and inhibits AgRP neurons (Takahashi and Cone, 2005) leading to reduced food consumption and increased energy expenditure.
evidence: Inferred from the combined effects of leptin on POMC and AgRP neurons, supported by citations.

claim: The ubiquitously expressed JNK1 and JNK2 isoforms play an important role in the metabolic stress response of peripheral tissues.
source: Previous studies have established that the ubiquitously expressed JNK1 and JNK2 isoforms play an important role in the metabolic stress response of peripheral tissues (Sabio and Davis, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio and Davis, 2010.

claim: Feeding a HFD causes activation of the ubiquitously expressed isoforms JNK1 and JNK2 in peripheral tissues, including liver, muscle, and adipose tissue.
source: It is established that feeding a HFD causes activation of the ubiquitously expressed isoforms JNK1 and JNK2 in peripheral tissues, including liver, muscle, and adipose tissue (Sabio and Davis, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio and Davis, 2010.

claim: JNK1 and JNK2 in neurons are constitutively activated and are primarily localized to axons and dendrites.
source: However, the regulation of JNK caused by feeding a HFD in the central nervous system is unclear because these ubiquitously expressed JNK isoforms in neurons are constitutively activated and are primarily localized to axons and dendrites (Coffey et al., 2000; Oliva et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coffey et al., 2000 and Oliva et al., 2006.

claim: JNK3 exhibits low basal activity and can be activated in the nucleus when neurons are exposed to environmental stress.
source: In contrast, the neuron-specific isoform JNK3 exhibits low basal activity and can be activated in the nucleus when neurons are exposed to environmental stress (Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 1997.

claim: JNK3 is required for stress-induced cJun phosphorylation and AP-1 activation in neurons.
source: Studies of Mapk10-/- mice demonstrate that JNK3 is required for stress-induced cJun phosphorylation and AP-1 activation in neurons (Yang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 1997.

claim: The role of JNK3 in neurons is non-redundant with JNK1 and JNK2.
source: This role of JNK3 in neurons is non-redundant with JNK1 and JNK2.
evidence: Inferred from the unique properties and functions of JNK3 compared to JNK1/2.

claim: JNK3 in LEPRb+ neurons regulates feeding behavior in mice.
source: Here we report that JNK3 in LEPRb+ neurons regulates feeding behavior in mice (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from LepRΔJ3 mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mechanism of JNK3 function requires metabolic stress (e.g. feeding a HFD) to cause JNK3 activation.
source: The mechanism of JNK3 function requires metabolic stress (e.g. feeding a HFD) to cause JNK3 activation.
evidence: Inferred from the diet-dependent phenotype and JNK3 activation data.

claim: JNK3 deficiency does not cause hyperphagia when mice are fed a chow diet.
source: Thus, JNK3 deficiency does not cause hyperphagia when mice are fed a chow diet, but JNK3 deficiency does cause hyperphagia when mice are fed a HFD.
evidence: Supported by food consumption data comparing CD and HFD feeding in Mapk10-/- mice.

claim: JNK3 deficiency causes hyperphagia when mice are fed a HFD.
source: Thus, JNK3 deficiency does not cause hyperphagia when mice are fed a chow diet, but JNK3 deficiency does cause hyperphagia when mice are fed a HFD.
evidence: Supported by food consumption data for HFD-fed Mapk10-/- mice.

claim: PTPN1-deficiency causes hypophagia on both CD and HFD.
source: In contrast, PTPN1-deficiency causes hypophagia on both CD and HFD (Bence et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bence et al., 2006.

claim: JNK3 is not required for fine-tuning leptin receptor signaling.
source: This analysis indicates that JNK3 is not required for fine-tuning leptin receptor signaling, but JNK3 is essential for determining the leptin signaling response during exposure to metabolic stress.
evidence: Inferred from the diet-specific phenotype of JNK3 deficiency.

claim: JNK3 is essential for determining the leptin signaling response during exposure to metabolic stress.
source: This analysis indicates that JNK3 is not required for fine-tuning leptin receptor signaling, but JNK3 is essential for determining the leptin signaling response during exposure to metabolic stress.
evidence: Inferred from the HFD-specific effects of JNK3 deficiency on leptin signaling.

claim: JNK3 serves a key role in the establishment of the set-point for the threshold of leptin signaling that controls feeding behavior in response to metabolic stress.
source: JNK3 therefore serves a key role in the establishment of the set-point for the threshold of leptin signaling that controls feeding behavior in response to metabolic stress.
evidence: Inferred from the role of JNK3 in regulating leptin signaling specifically during metabolic stress.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons is sufficient to cause HFD hyperphagia.
source: These data demonstrate that JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons is sufficient to cause HFD hyperphagia, although possible roles for JNK3 in other LEPRb+ neurons cannot be excluded by this analysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AgrpΔJ3 mice showing increased HFD consumption.

claim: Orexigenic signaling by AgRP neurons contributes to the effects of JNK3 deficiency on HFD hyperphagia.
source: We conclude that orexigenic signaling by AgRP neurons contributes to the effects of JNK3 deficiency on HFD hyperphagia.
evidence: Inferred from the sufficiency of JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons to cause hyperphagia.

claim: JNK3 deficiency in AgRP neurons causes an increase in mEPSC amplitude, but not frequency, in HFD-fed mice.
source: Our recordings measured glutamatergic transmission from all inputs to AgRP neurons and demonstrated an increase in mEPSC amplitude, but not frequency, from HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice compared with HFD-fed control mice (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The increase in mEPSC amplitude in JNK3-deficient AgRP neurons is consistent with a possible postsynaptic function of JNK3 in AgRP neurons.
source: This observation is consistent with a possible postsynaptic function of JNK3 in AgRP neurons whereby JNK3 affects AMPA and/or NMDA receptor activity within these neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the change in amplitude without change in frequency, suggesting postsynaptic mechanisms.

claim: Glutamatergic input to AgRP neurons stimulates feeding behavior.
source: Interestingly, glutamatergic input to AgRP neurons stimulates feeding behavior (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: The JNK scaffold proteins JIP1/2 can regulate NMDA receptor signaling.
source: For example, the JNK scaffold proteins JIP1/2 can regulate NMDA receptor signaling (Kennedy et al., 2007) and AMPA receptor phosphorylation by JNK regulates AMPA receptor function and trafficking (Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kennedy et al., 2007.

claim: AMPA receptor phosphorylation by JNK regulates AMPA receptor function and trafficking.
source: For example, the JNK scaffold proteins JIP1/2 can regulate NMDA receptor signaling (Kennedy et al., 2007) and AMPA receptor phosphorylation by JNK regulates AMPA receptor function and trafficking (Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomas et al., 2008.

claim: JNK-mediated AMPA receptor regulation may contribute to the hyperphagic phenotype of HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice.
source: Nevertheless, since an increased AMPA response was detected in JNK3-deficient AgRP neurons (Figure 6H and Figure 6-figure supplement 1), we conclude that JNK-mediated AMPA receptor regulation (Thomas et al., 2008) may contribute to the hyperphagic phenotype of HFD-fed JNK3-deficient mice.
evidence: Inferred from the increased AMPA response and known JNK regulation of AMPA receptors, supported by citation.

claim: JNK3 plays a major role in the regulation of energy balance.
source: The results of the present study indicate that JNK3 plays a major role in the regulation of energy balance.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in JNK3-deficient mice related to feeding and metabolism.

claim: The function of JNK3 to regulate feeding behavior differs from the roles of JNK1/JNK2 to regulate energy expenditure and insulin resistance.
source: This function of JNK3 to regulate feeding behavior differs from the roles of JNK1/JNK2 to regulate energy expenditure and insulin resistance (Sabio and Davis, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio and Davis, 2010 and comparison with JNK3 function.

claim: JNK1-deficient (Mapk8-/-) mice do not exhibit altered feeding behavior.
source: Since JNK1-deficient (Mapk8-/-) mice do not exhibit altered feeding behavior (Sabio et al., 2008) and endogenous JNK1 is constitutively activated in neurons (Coffey, 2014), it is unclear why transgenic over-expression of an activated Mapk8 allele (encoding a MKK7-JNK1 fusion protein) in WT mice would cause a small change in feeding behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio et al., 2008.

claim: Endogenous JNK1 is constitutively activated in neurons.
source: Since JNK1-deficient (Mapk8-/-) mice do not exhibit altered feeding behavior (Sabio et al., 2008) and endogenous JNK1 is constitutively activated in neurons (Coffey, 2014), it is unclear why transgenic over-expression of an activated Mapk8 allele (encoding a MKK7-JNK1 fusion protein) in WT mice would cause a small change in feeding behavior.
evidence: Supported by citation to Coffey, 2014.

claim: JNK1 and JNK2 do not influence feeding behavior.
source: On balance, we favor the conclusion that JNK1 and JNK2 do not influence feeding behavior (Sabio and Davis, 2010), but JNK3 promotes leptin-mediated suppression of HFD feeding behavior (when JNK3 is activated), but not CD feeding behavior (when JNK3 is inactive).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio and Davis, 2010 and inference from loss-of-function studies.

claim: JNK3 promotes leptin-mediated suppression of HFD feeding behavior (when JNK3 is activated), but not CD feeding behavior (when JNK3 is inactive).
source: On balance, we favor the conclusion that JNK1 and JNK2 do not influence feeding behavior (Sabio and Davis, 2010), but JNK3 promotes leptin-mediated suppression of HFD feeding behavior (when JNK3 is activated), but not CD feeding behavior (when JNK3 is inactive).
evidence: Inferred from the diet-specific effects of JNK3 deficiency on feeding behavior.

claim: JNK1 and JNK2 promote obesity by inhibiting energy expenditure.
source: The observation that JNK1 and JNK2 promote obesity (by inhibiting energy expenditure) and cause insulin resistance in peripheral tissues indicates that drugs that block JNK signaling may be therapeutically beneficial for the treatment of pre-diabetes (Sabio and Davis, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio and Davis, 2010.

claim: JNK1 and JNK2 cause insulin resistance in peripheral tissues.
source: The observation that JNK1 and JNK2 promote obesity (by inhibiting energy expenditure) and cause insulin resistance in peripheral tissues indicates that drugs that block JNK signaling may be therapeutically beneficial for the treatment of pre-diabetes (Sabio and Davis, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabio and Davis, 2010.

claim: Drugs that block JNK signaling may be therapeutically beneficial for the treatment of pre-diabetes.
source: The observation that JNK1 and JNK2 promote obesity (by inhibiting energy expenditure) and cause insulin resistance in peripheral tissues indicates that drugs that block JNK signaling may be therapeutically beneficial for the treatment of pre-diabetes (Sabio and Davis, 2010).
evidence: Inferred from the roles of JNK1/2 in obesity and insulin resistance, supported by citation.

claim: JNK3 inhibition causes HFD-dependent hyperphagia.
source: However, this study demonstrates that JNK3 inhibition causes HFD-dependent hyperphagia (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by food consumption data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Hyperphagia may result from JNK3 inhibition, representing a potential problem for drug therapy.
source: This represents a potential problem for drug therapy. While JNK1/2 inhibition may be therapeutically beneficial, hyperphagia may therefore result from JNK3 inhibition.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the implications of JNK3 inhibition for drug therapy.

claim: The most effective drug strategy for the treatment of pre-diabetes may require a small molecule that inhibits JNK1/2, but not JNK3.
source: Consequently, the most effective drug strategy for the treatment of pre-diabetes may require a small molecule that inhibits JNK1/2, but not JNK3.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about optimal drug design based on the differential roles of JNK isoforms.
